claims.text: The target component has a microstructure susceptible to hot cracking during high-temperature repair.
Localized friction stir deposition can mechanically incorporate a wear-resistant alloy powder into a damaged surface.
The friction-based deposition process operates at sub-melting temperatures.
The intervention produces a refined surface layer with strong bonding to the substrate.
The deposited layer contains a uniform dispersion of wear-resistant particles in a fine-grained matrix.
The refined, bonded surface layer minimizes repair-induced residual stresses.
The refined, bonded surface layer reduces hot-cracking tendencies.
Friction stir deposition induces severe plastic deformation.
Severe plastic deformation refines the surface microstructure.
Friction stir deposition promotes metallurgical bonding without melting the material.
The introduced wear-resistant phase increases surface hardness and durability.
Wear-resistant particles impede crack initiation and propagation.
The intervention reduces hot-cracking risk relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
The treated surface will have statistically significantly higher hardness than both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The treated surface will delay crack initiation relative to both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The intervention will improve corrosion resistance relative to traditional fusion-welding repair and untreated surfaces.
Hardness and wear resistance are expected to improve by approximately 20–30%.
The approach is expected to be effective only for localized damage and alloy systems compatible with friction stir processing.
Repair efficacy may diminish for extensive damage.
Repair efficacy may diminish for materials that are highly sensitive to mechanical deformation.
